idiom_name: one method per rule on a parser class over a token list (javac-shaped)
implementation_notes: The Java Language Specification splits the language into a lexical grammar (§2.2) and a syntactic grammar whose goal symbol is CompilationUnit (§2.3) - exactly the token stream plus parser structure recursive descent assumes - and javac's own parser (com.sun.tools.javac.parser.JavacParser) is a hand-written implementation of that grammar. In application code: a token record or enum plus a List<Token>, a Parser class with an index and peek/accept/expect helpers, one method per rule returning AST nodes, and a ParseException or a diagnostics list for errors, with switch expressions over token kinds keeping dispatch compact. Nothing in the JDK replaces the structure, so the hand-written form is the realization; move to ANTLR or JavaCC only when the grammar outgrows what hand-written rules keep readable.
pitfalls: Java has no tail-call elimination and a fixed thread stack: a rule-per-production parser must guard recursion depth explicitly or deeply nested input throws StackOverflowError.
Exceptions are the natural error path, but throwing on the first mismatch precludes recovery; javac logs diagnostics and synthesises error nodes instead, which is the shape IDE tooling needs.
List<Token> plus boxed kinds allocate on every access; an array of tokens with an int-encoded kind is the hot-path alternative.
